evidence_items.claim: New heavens and new earth echo Isaiah and may emphasize transformation, renewal, or replacement differently; righteousness dwelling there is the ethical center.
The compressed phrase new creation may describe a person in Messiah, a transformed mode of perception and relation, or the inbreaking renewal of creation.

Great White Throne Judgment unfolds within concrete settings such as Israelite kinship life, temple worship, royal courts, wilderness travel, Roman administration, or imperial conflict, depending on the passage.

Historically, Great White Throne Judgment is located by its canonical setting; this entry connects that setting with revelation, new-jerusalem, new-creation-theme and related CKL objects for contextual retrieval.

Isaiah 25-27 and 65-66 use death-defeat, bodily revival, transformed longevity, renewed Jerusalem, and new-heavens-and-earth imagery that becomes foundational for later Jewish and Christian resurrection and new-creation hope.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete sixty-six-chapter witness broadly aligned with the Masoretic tradition but containing thousands of orthographic and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and pesharim show active transmission and interpretation.

Responsible interpretation distinguishes a passage's literary sense and historical referent from prediction claims, typology, quotation, allusion, canonical synthesis, Jewish reception, and later christological or ecclesial readings.

Ancient background for New Jerusalem Prophecy includes royal courts, sanctuary worship, covenant lawsuits, exile, and restoration hope; the entry ties that world to Isaiah 65:17-25, Isaiah 66:22-24, new-jerusalem-theme, and new-creation-theme without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
The vision grows from exile and temple loss into a picture of final dwelling and restored holiness.
The vision reuses city and temple imagery familiar in the ancient world while transforming them around God’s direct presence.
New Jerusalem appears as the final hope of the biblical story, reshaping Zion imagery after judgment and exile.
